title: QuASAR: Toward an LLM-Assisted Framework for Screening, Prototyping, and Assessing Quantum-Advantage Opportunities in Scientific Computing
authors: Mark L. Carroll, Jordan A. Caraballo-Vega, Brian P. Powell, John L. Schnase
abstract: Identifying scientific computations that could benefit from quantum algorithms requires both domain knowledge and fluency in quantum algorithm design, expertise that rarely resides in one person. We report results from QuASAR, an experimental, two-agent, LLM-driven pipeline intended to bridge this gap. One agent screens scientific literature for computational kernels with a plausible quantum-algorithmic analogue and proposes candidates, each backed by citations. A second agent independently verifies those citations. For candidates that survive verification, it reconstructs the source's computational structure, formulates a quantum mapping, builds and executes a prototype, and benchmarks it against classical baselines. We applied this pipeline to ten candidate computations drawn from the astrophysics literature. Nine candidates were carried through to a small-scale, benchmarked prototype. We report three in detail, chosen as the clearest examples with the least redundancy across the set. They span combinatorial optimization, stochastic simulation, and Bayesian inference. The pipeline attempted to supply quantum-design expertise a domain scientist might lack, reconstructing source algorithms where one existed and building original, disclosed mappings where none did. None of the three case studies achieved quantum advantage at the tested scales, and their astrophysical framing has not yet undergone expert validation. What the experiment does show is that the pipeline can turn a published idea into a runnable prototype, which a scientist can then inspect, test against classical methods, and decide whether to pursue. QuASAR is an exploratory framework, offered to the community for evaluation, critique, and further development, with an approach that could broaden the use of quantum computing in scientific research and extend to computational improvements more generally.

infographic.key_insight: QuASAR uses two LLM agents to turn literature-derived scientific computations into runnable quantum prototypes, enabling exploration rather than demonstrating quantum advantage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help scientific computing teams screen quantum-algorithm opportunities and benchmark prototypes before committing specialist effort.
method: Screen scientific literature for computational kernels with plausible quantum analogues and supporting citations.
Independently verify citations, reconstruct computational structure, and formulate quantum mappings.
Build and execute prototypes, then benchmark against classical baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of ten astrophysics-derived candidates, nine reached small-scale benchmarked prototypes; three detailed case studies covered combinatorial optimization, stochastic simulation, and Bayesian inference.
infographic.watch_item: None of the three detailed cases achieved quantum advantage at tested scales, and their astrophysical framing still requires expert validation.
infographic.paper_title: QuASAR: Toward an LLM-Assisted Framework for Screening, Prototyping, and Assessing Quantum-Advantage Opportunities in Scientific Computing

title: Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process
authors: Rayane Ammar Khodja, Alexandre Voisin, Victor Costa, Fanny Casteran, Benoit Celse, Benoît Iung
abstract: Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. It learns adjacency matrices through Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and integrates spatial modelling with temporal encoding to represent process dynamics under evolving OCs. This paper evaluates the framework's foundational components (fault detection, GATv2 spatial graph learning and temporal encoding) on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, training only on fault-free data. The architecture achieves competitive detection from reconstruction error alone, with similarity-based feature selection improving both accuracy and graph structure diversity. We then evaluate the physical interpretability of the learned attention matrices against 22 ground-truth sensor pairs derived from the TEP control structure and process topology. GATv2 attention fails to recover all known physical pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a structural limitation of reconstruction-driven attention rather than a tuning issue. This challenges a common assumption in GNN-based FDD: that learned attention weights provide a basis for fault diagnosis and root-cause analysis. The architecture detects faults effectively, but the learned graph does not encode the physical topology needed for interpretable diagnosis, motivating physics-informed graph construction.

infographic.key_insight: The spatiotemporal GNN detects process faults effectively, but its learned attention graphs do not reliably recover physical relationships needed for interpretable diagnosis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers should validate fault-detection performance separately from graph interpretability before using attention weights for root-cause analysis.
method: Model operating-condition-specific normal subspaces linked by transition functions.
Combine GATv2 spatial graph learning with temporal encoding.
Propose reconstruction and Deep SVDD objectives; evaluate foundational components using fault-free training data.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the Tennessee Eastman Process benchmark, reconstruction error yielded competitive detection, while attention graphs failed to recover all 22 known physical sensor pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish the full framework's robustness to changing operating conditions; physics-informed graphs remain a proposed direction for interpretable diagnosis.
infographic.paper_title: Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process

title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search
authors: Yi Ding, Gaurav Kumar, Rui Min, Isabella Ye, Bhavika Goyal, Emilio Antunez
abstract: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. Tier 1 (Macro System) acts as a scalable user sentiment regression detector, utilizing a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM (based on Gemini XS) on telemetry features. Through multi-task regularization and contextual feature engineering, this tier achieves a +9.8% PR-AUC gain on over 500,000 held-out records, matching baseline recall on all validated regressions with $\sim$20% relative precision gain among the 12 held-out experiments. In production, it reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. Tier 2 (Micro System) provides granular diagnostics by employing a Multimodal LLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) to natively assess visual renderings and spatial layout of web result blocks, quantifying "User Toil" as the estimated effort required to reach a satisfactory result. Enhanced by RL-based automated prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns, the MLLM yields a $>$6.5% F1 score improvement, offering deep insights into content quality and layout friction. Ultimately, this framework enables scalable, accurate, and diagnostic UX attribution, processing O(100k) live experiment queries daily.

infographic.key_insight: A dual-tier framework combines telemetry-based sentiment regression detection with multimodal layout diagnostics to identify web-search UX problems at scale.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture supports faster A/B-test evaluation and targeted UX debugging while reducing reliance on surveys.
method: Macro tier: fine-tune a Gemini XS–based encoder-decoder model on telemetry using multi-task regularization and contextual features.
Micro tier: use Gemini 3.0 Pro to assess rendered results and spatial layout, estimating effort as “User Toil.”
Refine micro-tier diagnostics with RL-based prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports +9.8% PR-AUC on over 500,000 held-out records, approximately 20% relative precision gain at matched baseline recall across 12 held-out experiments, and >6.5% F1 improvement for the multimodal tier.
infographic.watch_item: Validate model-derived sentiment and User Toil against human judgments across changing search layouts; the abstract does not establish generalization beyond the reported setting.
infographic.paper_title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search

title: Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR): A Robust Framework for Estimating Spatially Varying Covariate Effects in Surrogate-Augmented Neuroimaging
authors: Guannan Wang, Yang Long, Shan Yu, Zhiling Gu, Lily Wang
abstract: Relating demographic, clinical, and genetic covariates to high-dimensional imaging outcomes is a core problem in brain imaging, especially when the target modality is observed for only a subset of participants. Generative models can synthesize missing modalities from auxiliary data, but using synthetic images in regression requires care to ensure valid inference. We propose a two-stage Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR) framework for spatially varying covariate effects under partially observed imaging outcomes. By calibrating surrogate information against observed target images, SSFR improves efficiency while remaining robust to discrepancies between the surrogate and target regression functions. We establish consistency and the convergence rate of the estimator, and show that first-stage surrogate-model estimation error does not alter its asymptotic rate. We introduce a voxelwise surrogate explanatory measure $R^2(z)$, the fraction of residual target-image variation explained by a candidate surrogate; with the observation rate, it gives a principled criterion for surrogate screening and indicates the potential efficiency gain. We further develop a weighted bootstrap procedure for simultaneous confidence corridors (SCCs). As surrogate informativeness increases, SCC widths approach those obtained under complete observation, improving localization of significant effects that cannot be identified from the observed data alone. Simulations confirm accuracy and robustness under surrogate misspecification and with surrogates generated by image-to-image neural networks. Applied to spatially normalized PET images from ADNI, SSFR yields interpretable coefficient maps and uniformly narrower SCCs than an analysis using observed PET alone, enlarging the region over which age-related metabolic decline is simultaneously significant.

infographic.key_insight: SSFR calibrates synthetic imaging surrogates against observed target images to estimate spatially varying covariate effects more precisely while remaining robust to surrogate–target regression discrepancies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables generative imaging models to support statistical inference when target scans are only partially observed, rather than treating synthetic scans as real measurements.
method: Use two-stage functional regression to calibrate surrogate information against observed target images.
Screen candidate surrogates using voxelwise residual explanatory power R²(z) together with the target-image observation rate.
Construct simultaneous confidence corridors using a weighted bootstrap.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations assessed accuracy and robustness, including neural-network-generated surrogates; an ADNI PET application produced uniformly narrower confidence corridors and a larger region of simultaneously significant age-related metabolic decline than observed-PET-only analysis.
infographic.watch_item: Efficiency gains depend on surrogate informativeness and the observation rate; robustness to regression discrepancies does not imply protection against arbitrary missing-data mechanisms.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR): A Robust Framework for Estimating Spatially Varying Covariate Effects in Surrogate-Augmented Neuroimaging

title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
authors: Mamoona Tasadduq, Maryam Bashir
abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.

infographic.key_insight: Ranking-preserving coresets accelerate evolutionary hyperparameter optimization by evaluating configurations on compact data subsets designed to preserve full-data performance rankings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusing a selected coreset can reduce repeated model-training costs while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-data optimization.
method: Evolve a coreset to maximize Spearman correlation between subset-based and full-data configuration rankings.
Penalize subset size to balance ranking fidelity against computational cost.
Run hyperparameter optimization on the coreset using GA, CHC, or PSO.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 11 tabular, text, and image datasets, HPO-stage speedups were approximately 1.14×–8.80×; on 20 held-out configurations, ranking correlation exceeded same-size random sampling on 8 datasets (Wilcoxon p = 0.014).
infographic.watch_item: HPO-stage speedups exclude one-time coreset construction; assess end-to-end runtime and the number of reuse runs needed to break even.
infographic.paper_title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization

title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
authors: Kasidit Srimahajariyapong, Thiparat Chotibut, Suwannachad Suwannajitt, Tithivich Paka, Ricard Puig, Yudai Suzuki
abstract: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

infographic.key_insight: Riemannian gradient optimization enables autonomous quantum model training without intermediate quantum measurements or classical feedback under sufficient conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could remove the quantum–classical training bottleneck, shifting implementation challenges toward quantum circuit depth and autonomous update realization.
method: Derive Riemannian gradient updates for a broad class of quantum learning tasks.
Identify conditions for fully autonomous quantum updates and prove exponential convergence for sufficiently small step sizes.
Analyze circuit-depth growth and discovery of hidden data symmetries without prior specification.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical studies of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry indicate learning at low circuit depths using only a few distinct training examples.
infographic.watch_item: Autonomous operation and convergence are conditional; the abstract does not establish hardware performance or robustness to quantum noise.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization

title: Do Alice and Bob Dream of the Oracle? Wishful Cryptanalysis
authors: Guoxiao Liu, Keting Jia, Hongbo Yu, Zongyue Wang, Tianshuo Cong, Junfeng Fan
abstract: For two millennia, offense and defense have forged cryptographic security boundaries. Tools automated calculation and search, while humans drove discovery. Foundation models now mark a shift from automated computation to intelligent scientific discovery. Because cryptanalysis rests on exact mathematical definitions and immediately executable truth, it offers a proving ground for autonomous intelligence to move past security reliant on scarce human attention and explore structures beyond human working memory. Unguided models stall between two opposite traps: authority hallucination, where they surrender whenever prior literature declares a route blocked, and reasoning hallucination, where they produce subtle, unverifiable flaws. Closed platforms and generic agent loops further impede sustained open inquiry. We introduce wishful cryptanalysis, a harness-agnostic methodology that pairs constructive optimism against entrenched assumptions with blinded, zero-import verification against error. Agents first compress reduced-scale theory within provisioned compute so live witnesses certify their mathematics automatically. They then co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, and climb parameter ladders toward high-round theory. Applied across frontier open-weight and proprietary models with minimal human intervention beyond targets and compute, this paradigm yielded novel attack techniques and thirteen verifiable practical results across Keccak (SHA-3) and AES. These include breaking a fifteen-year-open public challenge and closing longstanding practical gaps, released alongside an early-preview open-source workbench (agent-framework). Extending Kerckhoffs's principle into the AI era, we envision an Open Oracle, an open and auditable public infrastructure that frees cryptographers to legislate security goals, challenge assumptions, distill theory, and co-design resilient standards.

infographic.key_insight: Wishful cryptanalysis pairs exploratory AI reasoning with executable verification to discover cryptanalytic attacks without deferring blindly to prior literature.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The methodology offers a harness-agnostic approach to AI-assisted security research that co-adapts cryptographic primitives, attack algorithms, and hardware within provisioned compute.
method: Develop reduced-scale theory with executable witnesses that certify mathematical claims.
Pair constructive optimism with blinded, zero-import verification to catch flawed reasoning.
Co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, then climb parameter ladders toward higher-round attacks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports thirteen verifiable practical results across Keccak (SHA-3) and AES using open-weight and proprietary models, including resolution of a fifteen-year-open public challenge.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify attack parameters, compute costs, or verification details; these results should not be read as breaks of full standardized SHA-3 or AES.
infographic.paper_title: Do Alice and Bob Dream of the Oracle? Wishful Cryptanalysis

title: Solving the pre-image problem in kernel PCA: The reproducing property is all you need
authors: Joel-Pascal Ntwali N'konzi, Stefan Klus
abstract: Kernel PCA extends PCA to nonlinear dimensionality reduction by implicitly mapping data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) via the kernel trick, with applications ranging from image denoising to out-of-distribution detection. While its projection map is well understood, appropriately defining the associated reconstruction map is a longstanding challenge since projecting back from the RKHS to the input space is non-trivial. This is known as the pre-image problem. Existing approaches have tackled this problem by either relying on nonlinear optimization, which is prone to numerical instabilities and sensitive to initialization, or by solving a separate supervised learning problem, incurring additional computational overhead. Furthermore, although the projection map of kernel PCA reduces to that of standard PCA when a linear kernel is used, most of these approaches are not guaranteed to recover PCA's reconstruction map in this case, a consistency property that one would naturally expect to hold. In this paper, we leverage the reproducing property of the RKHS to derive a reconstruction map for kernel PCA that is provably consistent. Our derivations rely on the mild assumption that the RKHS either contains linear functions or the kernel is universal, which holds for standard kernels. We further extend the method to the random Fourier features (RFFs) approximation of kernel PCA by introducing a corresponding notion of RFF reproducing property. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs comparably with state-of-the-art methods across kernel choices, while remaining more computationally efficient and maintaining consistent performance in settings where these baseline methods drastically fail.

infographic.key_insight: The RKHS reproducing property yields a kernel PCA reconstruction map that provably recovers standard PCA reconstruction when a linear kernel is used.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a computationally efficient reconstruction approach for kernel PCA applications such as image denoising and out-of-distribution detection.
method: Derive reconstruction using the RKHS reproducing property.
Assume the RKHS contains linear functions or the kernel is universal.
Extend reconstruction to random Fourier features through a corresponding reproducing property.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods across kernel choices, with greater computational efficiency and robustness in settings where baselines fail.
infographic.watch_item: Verify that the chosen kernel satisfies the theoretical assumptions; the abstract provides no quantitative runtime or reconstruction-error results.
infographic.paper_title: Solving the pre-image problem in kernel PCA: The reproducing property is all you need

title: Closed-loop policy optimisation for cylinder wake control via differentiable simulation
authors: Siwen Zhang, Xizeng Zhao, Zhouteng Ye, Yulin Xie, Zesheng Yao
abstract: Suppressing vortex shedding behind a circular cylinder is a classical problem in active flow control.Model-free deep reinforcement learning (DRL) learns such policies by interacting with the flow without differentiating its dynamics, which typically requires a large interaction budget. This study optimises closed-loop policies by differentiable simulation: control-loss gradients propagate through the simulated flow to the policy parameters, which are updated by reverse-mode automatic differentiation. The policy maps local velocity measurements to a jet amplitude imposed through differentiable synthetic-jet boundary conditions. In a two-dimensional confined cylinder wake at Rey=100, eight policy updates (about 78 shedding periods of forward simulation) give approximately 8% drag reduction and 99.6% suppression of lift fluctuations, the drag level being comparable to reported DRL results. Suppression is sustained by feedback: a mean-matched constant jet does not maintain it, whereas the same policy responds similarly at three activation phases and recovers after upstream disturbances. A velocity-deviation reward alone retains strong suppression, and observations of two instantaneous velocity components at one near-wake or surface location reach about 99.8% suppression, whereas a single surface pressure leaves residual oscillations. Together with related DRL results, this suggests that reward and observation requirements here are set by policy optimisation and flow physics.

infographic.key_insight: Differentiating through a simulated cylinder wake enables closed-loop policy optimisation that strongly suppresses vortex shedding with only eight policy updates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation gradients offer a potentially interaction-efficient route to feedback flow control with synthetic jets and sparse local velocity sensing.
method: Map local velocity measurements to synthetic-jet amplitude with a feedback policy.
Backpropagate control-loss gradients through differentiable flow simulation to update policy parameters.
Test feedback dependence, activation phases, disturbance recovery, rewards and sensor choices.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a two-dimensional confined wake at Reynolds number 100, eight updates using about 78 shedding periods of forward simulation achieved approximately 8% drag reduction and 99.6% suppression of lift fluctuations.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to a two-dimensional simulated wake at Reynolds number 100; robustness in three-dimensional, higher-Reynolds-number or physical flows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Closed-loop policy optimisation for cylinder wake control via differentiable simulation

title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
authors: Kaden Zheng, Pratyusha Sharma
abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.

infographic.key_insight: Model Carving jointly learns Transformer weights and topology, yielding smaller, heterogeneous models that outperform fixed-architecture baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Removing sublayers during training reduces inference cost, with reported savings of up to 34% in FLOPs per token and up to 1.6× faster decoding without quality loss.
method: Attach learnable scalar gates to attention and MLP sublayers.
Let the training loss drive sublayer removal while optimizing model weights.
Retain the resulting smaller, heterogeneous network for inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on standard Transformers spanning 140M–2.7B parameters and looped Transformers spanning 140M–1.3B, carved models achieved lower validation loss than dense baselines trained with up to 1.7× more compute and outperformed size-matched pruned or distilled models.
infographic.watch_item: Real-world speedups should be verified on target hardware, since FLOP reductions do not guarantee proportional latency improvements.
infographic.paper_title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology

title: SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement
authors: Huaze Tang, Runqing Miao, Tianren Peng, Lam Nguyen, Chao Wang, Jairong Li
abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.

infographic.key_insight: SUAF compresses action-dependent predictions of future visitation into leading spectral features that support reward-independent, zero-shot policy improvement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agents can reuse learned features across reward functions, with spectral truncation providing a principled way to manage representation capacity and approximation error.
method: Construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix under a reference policy.
Retain leading singular modes to approximate delayed advantages through linear reward projections, keeping immediate reward contrasts separate.
Learn features from reward-free data using action-centered Soft-HGR and bidirectional temporal-difference estimation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports finite-state validation of spectral predictions and feature learning, plus zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks, without quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Policy-improvement guarantees require sufficient error conditions; retaining leading modes alone does not guarantee improvement for every reward.
infographic.paper_title: SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement

title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
authors: Maximilian Rokuss, Jeya Maria Jose Valanarasu, Alejandro Lozano, Benjamin Hamm, Yannick Kirchhoff, Fabian Isensee
abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

infographic.key_insight: LesionAgent combines an LLM with frozen 3D imaging tools and a structured verification harness to track tumors and assess treatment response without task-specific training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results suggest that tool orchestration, persistent lesion memory, and deterministic clinical rules can matter more than the choice of LLM for reliable imaging workflows.
method: Operates frozen 3D detection, segmentation, registration, and tracking models through coordinate-labelled views.
Maintains a longitudinal lesion registry and verifies model outputs before relying on them.
Delegates numerical response assessment to a deterministic clinical-guideline engine.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four public longitudinal CT datasets, it outperformed automatic baselines in tracking and measurement; false progression calls fell from 33/56 with fixed-rule chaining to 2/56, and clinical response agreement reached 20/23 follow-ups.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical response evaluation covered only 23 follow-ups; broader prospective validation is needed before routine deployment.
infographic.paper_title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT

title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
authors: Chrisantus Eze
abstract: Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present \sys{}, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs.\ 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], $p = 5.82 \times 10^{-8}$) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0\% vs.\ 15.4\%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta ($\DB$) convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0\% vs.\ 62.5\% for Fixed-$3$) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4$\times$. Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7\% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9\% for a Self-Refine critic, $p = 0.61$) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. Across 200 runs on 40 research hypotheses evaluated with DeepSeek-R1-32B, \sys{} balances compute efficiency with rigorous epistemic verification.

infographic.key_insight: Asymmetric debate roles and evidence-based stopping make multi-agent research verification more compute-efficient while reducing role similarity and enabling auditable claim grounding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Research-verification pipelines can use opposing agent directives, convergence monitoring, and independent evidence checks instead of fixed-round debate.
method: Assign Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator roles with opposing epistemic directives.
Stop debate using the evidence-grounded Belief-Delta convergence criterion.
Anchor supported claims to verbatim literature snippets audited by an independent NLI classifier.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 200 runs on 40 hypotheses using DeepSeek-R1-32B, the framework reported 2.4× fewer LLM calls, 0% over-iteration versus 62.5% for Fixed-3, and a 21.7% hallucination rate.
infographic.watch_item: Hallucinations remained substantial and were not significantly lower than Self-Refine's 25.9% rate (p = 0.61); generalization beyond the evaluated model and hypotheses remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification

title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
authors: Samarth Sarin, Lovepreet Singh, Dhagash Mehta
abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph.

infographic.key_insight: Schema-driven extraction, temporal constraints, and source provenance enable auditable financial knowledge graphs whose quality can be evaluated independently of downstream retrieval.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The methodology offers a blueprint for preserving issuer identity, reporting periods, and evidence traceability when turning heterogeneous financial documents into structured knowledge.
method: Parse page-delimited documents and extract entities, quantitative observations, and relationships from overlapping windows using phased LLM processing.
Validate candidates against schemas and resolve entities with scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted matching.
Apply temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an evidence-grounded temporal graph and an intrinsic evaluation framework with seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics, but no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Intrinsic graph-quality evaluation does not by itself establish improvements in downstream retrieval or answer accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation

title: DistDNA: Language Model Fingerprinting under Stochastic Decoding
authors: Lifan Hu, Qian Yu, Zhaomin Wu, Bingsheng He
abstract: Behavioral fingerprints identify a large language model (LLM) from its responses to a shared set of prompts, enabling applications such as verifying whether a deployed model corresponds to the checkpoint it claims to be. Deployed models, however, are commonly served with stochastic decoding, under which the same model may produce different responses to an identical prompt, depending on an unknown temperature and top-$p$ setting. Existing representations such as LLM DNA provide limited treatment of this variation. A natural remedy is to characterize models by their response distributions, which, however, raises two challenges. First, each distribution must be estimated from only a small number of sampled responses. Second, a change in decoding setting can alter responses to the same extent as a change of checkpoint. Consequently, fingerprint distances alone provide an incomplete basis for model identity, and identification typically relies on a classifier trained jointly on fingerprints from many checkpoints. We propose DistDNA, which represents a model by its prompt-conditional response distributions and compares models by promptwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). The model under examination is assigned to the known checkpoint whose reference fingerprints, collected at several decoding settings, lie nearest to its own, without training a classifier. We show that finite sampling adds variance-dependent terms to the expected squared fingerprint distance, with these terms decreasing as $O(1/R)$ for equal response counts, where $R$ is the number of responses per prompt. Experiments across 115 model checkpoint entries demonstrate that DistDNA improves identification accuracy over the strongest baseline, LLM DNA, by 10.36%.

infographic.key_insight: DistDNA identifies LLM checkpoints under stochastic decoding by comparing response distributions rather than individual responses, without training an identity classifier.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It supports verification that a deployed LLM matches its claimed checkpoint despite unknown temperature and top-p settings.
method: Sample multiple responses to shared prompts to estimate prompt-conditional response distributions.
Compare fingerprints using promptwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD).
Assign the nearest known checkpoint using reference fingerprints collected at several decoding settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 115 model checkpoint entries, DistDNA improved identification accuracy over the strongest baseline, LLM DNA, by a reported 10.36%.
infographic.watch_item: Finite sampling adds variance-dependent distance terms that decrease as O(1/R), so reliable identification must balance responses per prompt against collection cost.
infographic.paper_title: DistDNA: Language Model Fingerprinting under Stochastic Decoding

title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
authors: Alessandro Piccolo, Francesco De Nicolò, Francesco Manco, Eufemia Lella
abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.

infographic.key_insight: The best zero-shot systems averaged about 1 macro-F1 point below target-dataset fine-tuned encoders, while OpenAI’s decision endpoint matched its underlying LLM at one-fifth the median latency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Without labeled training data, strong zero-shot systems offer a practical default, with decision models adding per-option probabilities and potentially lower latency.
method: Compare 3 decision models, 2 general-purpose LLMs, and 2 fine-tuned multilingual encoders.
Classify joy, sadness, anger, and fear using Italian instructions across 10 social-media datasets in 5 languages.
Evaluate macro-F1 with paired difference and equivalence tests, plus prompt and instruction-language sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The top zero-shot systems beat cross-dataset fine-tuned encoders by 8–15 macro-F1 points and showed about 1 point of standard deviation across prompts.
infographic.watch_item: Near-average parity is not proven equivalence: test sets cannot exclude a 4–5-point gap, individual-dataset differences reached 22 points, and fine-tuning won widely on GoEmotions.
infographic.paper_title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders

title: MetaRigor: From Agentic Automation to Verifiable End-to-End Meta-Analysis Through Scientific Decision Boundaries
authors: Yifeng Xie, Chenke Li, Yangshuo Miao, Jingyuan Zheng, Mingxuan Liu, Feiwei Qin
abstract: Automated meta-analysis requires not only accurate numerical extraction but also the consistent preservation of result identity across stages, including the associated study, comparison, population, outcome, time point, and analysis conditions. We present MetaRigor, an LLM workflow framework for verifiable end-to-end evidence synthesis. MetaRigor organizes study results as Study x Target units and operationalizes scientific decision boundaries at the task level through Task Contracts, programmatic rules, and source binding. The model performs semantic interpretation that depends on study context, whereas programs execute formalizable rules, computations, validation, and source verification. We conducted controlled evaluations across five stages: evidence acquisition, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, certainty of evidence assessment, and manuscript generation. MetaRigor achieved an F1 score of 86.29% for complete result delivery and 80.20% agreement for domain-level certainty of evidence judgments. Generated manuscripts received scores of 86.00 under human evaluation, exceeding all three baselines. A seven-case downstream end-to-end evaluation further yielded an aggregate F1 score of 77.01%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.78 percentage points. Cross-system tracing of archived outputs from three systems further showed that local mismatches or omissions in result identity could alter statistical inputs and the objects subjected to risk of bias assessment, with these errors subsequently propagating into the final report. Ablation experiments showed that task constraints and programmatic rules played distinct roles across different stages. These findings indicate that, in LLM-driven evidence synthesis workflows, consistently maintaining explicit result identity, decision boundaries, and provenance relationships is critical to improving end-to-end verifiability.

infographic.key_insight: MetaRigor makes automated meta-analysis more verifiable by preserving result identity and separating context-dependent scientific interpretation from programmable rules and checks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Research-agent pipelines should track study, comparison, population, outcome, time point, and analysis conditions explicitly to prevent local errors from propagating into final reports.
method: Organize results as Study × Target units with explicit identity and source binding.
Use Task Contracts to define scientific decision boundaries at each workflow stage.
Assign contextual interpretation to LLMs and formal rules, computation, validation, and source verification to programs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five evaluated stages, MetaRigor achieved 86.29% complete-result delivery F1 and 80.20% domain-level certainty agreement; seven end-to-end cases yielded 77.01% aggregate F1, 9.78 percentage points above the strongest baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The seven-case end-to-end evaluation provides limited evidence of generalizability; explicit contracts and provenance checks still require validation for new review settings.
infographic.paper_title: MetaRigor: From Agentic Automation to Verifiable End-to-End Meta-Analysis Through Scientific Decision Boundaries

title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs
authors: Manh V. Nguyen, Liang Zhao, Bobin Deng, Xinyue Zhang, Shaoen Wu
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL) lets ANN and SNN devices train collaboratively, benefiting both model types without requiring an all-neuromorphic deployment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: HNFL offers a path to gradually integrate neuromorphic Edge AI devices into existing federated learning systems.
method: Combine heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within one federated learning framework.
Train collaboratively to improve both ANN-based and SNN-based federated learning.
Evaluate VGG9 and ResNet architectures on CIFAR-10.
infographic.evidence_signal: CIFAR-10 experiments report average improvements of 16.85% when adding SNN devices to ANN-based FL and 8.02% in the reverse direction, plus spiking-activity reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports only CIFAR-10 evaluation; reduced spiking activity does not by itself establish measured device-level energy savings.
infographic.paper_title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs

title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning
authors: Umberto Biccari, Junqing Huang, Kang Liu, Enrique Zuazua
abstract: Generative models transform simple random inputs into samples that resemble observed data. For a finite training set, a central question is how its geometry shapes the terminal dynamics and the probabilities assigned to individual samples. We address this question for flow matching with linear interpolation between independent Gaussian and empirical samples. The squared distance to the training set generates explicit paths contracting exponentially toward the nearest sample. We prove that exact trajectories restarted at prescribed late-time states approximate these paths uniformly over all elapsed times and compact sets of starting states away from Voronoi interfaces, with an error exponentially small in the inverse squared restart noise scale. The initial mass near interfaces controls the quadratic Wasserstein error between the exact and reference laws. For Gaussian and fixed Gaussian-tube restart laws, this gives a square-root rate in the restart noise scale, uniform over time, which a two-site example shows to be sharp in general. At ties, the Clarke subdifferential characterizes the graphical limit of the rescaled velocity field. This geometry motivates two learning methods: fitting the distance potential with value and gradient supervision, and fitting velocities along explicit contraction paths. A transport estimate separates initialization mismatch, velocity error, incomplete contraction, and endpoint allocation. MNIST experiments illustrate the distinct roles of support proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity. These results connect flow matching and score-based diffusion through a common limiting geometry and show how asymptotic analysis can inform the design and evaluation of generative models.

infographic.key_insight: At late times, flow matching follows the geometry of the training set, approaching explicit paths that contract exponentially toward the nearest sample.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This geometry motivates simpler training targets and diagnostics that distinguish sample proximity, endpoint allocation, and feature fidelity.
method: Analyze linear-interpolation flow matching between independent Gaussian and empirical samples using the squared-distance potential.
Approximate late-time trajectories by explicit nearest-sample contraction paths away from Voronoi interfaces.
Learn either the distance potential with value-and-gradient supervision or velocities along contraction paths.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical bounds establish a uniform-in-time square-root Wasserstein rate under specified restart laws, a two-site example shows sharpness in general, and MNIST experiments illustrate distinct evaluation criteria.
infographic.watch_item: Near Voronoi interfaces, nearest-sample assignments are ambiguous, and restart mass near these boundaries controls distributional approximation error.
infographic.paper_title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning

title: BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics
authors: Michael Gastegger, Adam E. Foster, José Jiménez-Luna, Tim Hempel, Sarah Lewis, Yu Xie
abstract: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable.

infographic.key_insight: BioEmu2 unifies biomolecular structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution in a generative model that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It could accelerate computational studies of multi-component biomolecular systems, including binding, conformational changes and rare-state free energies.
method: Trains on experimental structures, synthetic structures and extensive molecular dynamics data.
Generates atomically resolved systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions.
Supports contact conditioning, bias-potential steering, enhanced sampling and context-parallel prediction of megadalton complexes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports structure accuracy comparable to leading open-weight folding models and free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol against molecular dynamics references across tested proteins and complexes.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy of equilibrium distributions and predicted kinetics on systems outside the tested set requires validation before replacing molecular dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics
